April 2014.

Election season.

Narendra Modi, Gujarat CM and BJP’s prime ministerial face, finally sits down with Doordarshan after years of alleged blackout.  

He tells the interviewer Gujarat poured maximum revenue into DD, yet the national broadcaster kept its distance. He speaks “only for the sake of democracy.”  

The interview runs nearly an hour.  
Recorded. Sent to Delhi.  

What airs on 27 April is shorter.  
Roughly half.  
Portions missing.  

Comments on Priyanka Gandhi.  
Remarks on Ahmed Patel.  
Gone.  

Controversy erupts.  
BJP alleges censorship.  
Doordarshan says technical cuts only.  

Then Jawhar Sircar, CEO of Prasar Bharati, writes to the Board.  

He admits:  
“It appears that while portions critical of Doordarshan were telecast, certain comments on other personalities were apparently edited.”  

He points to the long absence of real operational autonomy.
  
The Ministry of Information & Broadcasting still controls postings, transfers, and the News Division.  

He names the young minister Manish Tewari as having failed to break the old linkage that continued even after Prasar Bharati was created in 1997.  

Sircar says he himself gave the green signal to telecast despite no “balancing interview” from the other side.  

The letter becomes public.  
The shadow over the public broadcaster is confirmed by its own CEO.  

Modi later tweets on Press Freedom Day that the national channel is “struggling to maintain its professional freedom.”  

The interview that was meant to end a blackout instead opens a fresh chapter on who controls the microphone.
